styles.name: Socratic
styles.instructions: Lead with questions. Reveal one idea at a time. Let the student do the reasoning and respond to their attempt before adding anything.

styles.name: Examples first
styles.instructions: Show one fully worked example, then a similar problem with steps faded, then one unaided. Fade support as accuracy rises.

styles.name: Proof workshop
styles.instructions: The student drafts proofs; critique line by line. Name the gap and ask for the fix; never rewrite the proof for them.

styles.name: Quick quiz
styles.instructions: Rapid retrieval: short questions mixed from this and earlier checkpoints, immediate feedback, one-line explanations.

styles.name: Visual
styles.instructions: Build intuition first with pictures in words, concrete examples and counterexamples, then formalize.

styles.name: Short lecture
styles.instructions: Explain the idea in at most 150 words with one example, then check understanding with one question before moving on.

note.front: Why does a finite intersection of open neighborhoods remain open?
note.back: For each $x$ in the finite intersection choose an open neighborhood contained in every open set; the intersection of finitely many such neighborhoods is open.

note.front: Why is a compact subset of a Hausdorff space closed?
note.back: For each $x\notin K$, separate $x$ from each $y\in K$; a finite subcover of $K$ yields one neighborhood of $x$ disjoint from $K$.

note.front: Where is finiteness used when proving compact sets are closed in a Hausdorff space?
note.back: The intersection of finitely many neighborhoods of $x$ remains open, and it avoids the corresponding finite union covering $K$.

note.front: Does a closed subset of a compact space remain compact?
note.back: Yes: adjoin the open complement of the closed set to any relative open cover, then extract a finite subcover of the ambient compact space.

note.front: Give a compactness argument for a continuous image.
note.back: Pull back an open cover of $f(K)$ along continuous $f$, choose finitely many preimages covering $K$, then push those finitely many sets forward.

note.front: Is every compact set bounded in a metric space?
note.back: Yes: balls $B(x_0,n)$ for $n\in\mathbb N$ cover it; one member of a finite subcover supplies a uniform bound.

note.front: State the Heine–Borel theorem.
note.back: A subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.

note.front: State sequential compactness for metric spaces.
note.back: Every sequence has a convergent subsequence whose limit belongs to the space; this is equivalent to compactness for metric spaces.

note.front: Does compactness imply completeness in metric spaces?
note.back: Yes. A Cauchy sequence has a convergent subsequence by sequential compactness, forcing the whole sequence to converge.

note.front: Why is $\mathbb R$ not compact in its usual metric?
note.back: The open cover $\{(-n,n):n\in\mathbb N\}$ has no finite subcover.

note.front: Why does every convergent sequence in a metric space have a unique limit?
note.back: If $x_n\to a$ and $x_n\to b$, then $d(a,b)\le d(a,x_n)+d(x_n,b)\to0$.

note.front: What is the open-set characterization of continuity?
note.back: $f:X\to Y$ is continuous iff every open $U\subseteq Y$ has open preimage $f^{-1}(U)\subseteq X$.

note.front: State the sequential criterion for $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L$.
note.back: For every sequence $x_n\to a$ with $x_n\ne a$, one has $f(x_n)\to L$, assuming $a$ is an accumulation point.

note.front: Why is boundedness alone not enough for compactness?
note.back: The bounded set $(0,1)$ is not closed in $\mathbb R$, hence not compact by Heine–Borel.

note.front: What quantifier distinguishes uniform from pointwise continuity?
note.back: In uniform continuity $\delta$ depends only on $\varepsilon$, not on the base point $x$.

note.front: What compactness property proves the extreme value theorem?
note.back: The continuous image is compact in $\mathbb R$, hence closed and bounded, so it contains its supremum and infimum.

note.front: What is a separation of a topological space?
note.back: A decomposition into two disjoint nonempty relatively open sets whose union is the space.

note.front: Which topological property underlies the intermediate value theorem?
note.back: Intervals are connected, and continuous images preserve connectedness.

note.front: Prove a continuous bijection from compact to Hausdorff is a homeomorphism.
note.back: A continuous image of any closed subset of the compact domain is compact, hence closed in the Hausdorff codomain; the inverse is continuous.
